extracted.intended_audience: researchers, inventors, and patent practitioners seeking guidance on patenting natural products in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analysis of US patent eligibility, claim drafting, and disclosure strategies for extracts, isolated natural products, formulations, methods, and product-by-process claims in light of Myriad, Mayo, Chakrabarty, and USPTO 2014 guidance. Focuses on how to obtain enforceable patents for natural-product-derived inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exclusions for patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are excluded from patent-eligible protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural products discovered rather than invented are excluded; patent eligibility is distinct from patentability (novelty, inventiveness, industrial applicability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core patentability requirements (novelty, utility, inventiveness, industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be new and useful to be patentable; statutory requirements include novelty, inventiveness (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent eligibility (can seek protection) is separate from meeting these patentability requirements necessary to be granted a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Markedly different" / "significantly different" standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated natural product must be 'significantly' or 'markedly' different from what exists in nature to be patent-eligible; not all differences rise to the level of 'marked differences'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'marked difference must be a significant difference, i.e., more than an incidental or trivial difference' (USPTO guidance). Courts have required differences 'in kind' rather than merely 'in degree'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences weigh primary; functional differences secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural difference is a primary—but not sole—criterion for patent eligibility; functional differences may be considered but are not mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO guidance treats structural difference as important (e.g., synthetic derivative 5-methyl amazonic acid patent-eligible) while functional differences may or may not suffice for chemical products. Examples: isolated gene structure not deemed a 'marked' structural change in Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels like 'isolated', 'recombinant', 'synthetic' do not add patent-eligibility weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'isolated', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' add no weight to the patent eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely reciting such terms without substantive structural or marked functional changes will not make a claim patent-eligible under the USPTO standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic-material specifics: cDNA vs naturally occurring DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated genomic DNA with identical sequence to a natural gene is patent-ineligible; complementary DNA (cDNA) that lacks introns may be patentable because it is not naturally occurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short strands of cDNA indistinguishable from natural DNA may nonetheless be unpatentable; the Court focused on genetic information (sequence) not created by patentee in Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositions of multiple natural products must show 'marked' difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition combining natural products remains a product of nature if the combined products show no marked difference from the natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formulation may be patent-eligible if it includes additional element(s) that make the combination 'something significantly different' (e.g., enhanced efficacy at a lower dosage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-use claims require a practical, specific, significant application
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of using natural products should involve a practical, specific, and significant application so the claimed method would not foreclose others from using the same natural product in other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite (i) a general instruction to use the natural product; (ii) well-understood, purely conventional, or routine steps; or (iii) steps that anyone must use to apply the product are insufficient. Example: 'administer amazonic acid' may fail, whereas specifying a regimen/dosage (10–20 days at 0.76–1.25 teaspoons daily) could satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim limits and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Product-by-process' claims define a product by the process used to make it (e.g., 'product X obtained by process Y') and are accepted only when the product cannot otherwise be adequately defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S., patentability of a product-by-process claim is determined by the product itself regardless of the process; the process is considered only if it implies distinctive structural characteristics. If the product is identical or similar to known products, applicants bear the burden to show novelty/non-obviousness. Enforcement: such claims typically only cover products produced by the recited process, so an accused product made by a different process may not infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of manufacturing methods versus products
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing methods (e.g., extraction, preparation of drugs/supplements) remain patentable if they satisfy novelty and non-obviousness, even when the raw natural products are problematic for subject-matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on process claims as a viable avenue when products themselves are close to natural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient disclosure: written description and enablement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must sufficiently describe the invention so that one skilled in the art would recognize and be enabled to practice the invention; generic claims cannot be broader than what is enabled/disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to a general formula is not patentable if only a few species are disclosed—claims may be limited to explicitly described species. Disclose as many substitutions, modifications, and parameters (e.g., temperature, pH, reagents) as reasonably possible to support broader claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-drafting strategy: focus and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be drafted within a reasonable scope and be of sufficient significance so they do not appear to be a general application of the natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overbroad claims that simply claim the natural product; instead claim derivatives, modified structures, formulations, specific dosages/regimens, manufacturing processes, and particular applications to increase likelihood of eligibility and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice: include multiple claim types and detailed characterizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all features and available information that may characterize the products in the application and draft separate claims directed to the manufacturing process and the product-by-process for broader protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers are highly advised to include detailed descriptions of individual embodiments and combinations, and to draft both product and process claims to expand protection and mitigate risks of invalidation or narrow enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant burden when claimed product resembles known products
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed product is identical to or similar to a known product, the applicant bears the burden of proving novelty and non-obviousness to overcome prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is particularly important for product-by-process claims since U.S. law evaluates the product itself for novelty; patentees should be prepared to demonstrate distinguishing structural or marked functional characteristics.
